Halley's Comet. The most famous periodic comet in human history, visible from Earth roughly every 75 to 76 years. Named after astronomer Edmund Halley, who predicted its return in 1758 based on seventeenth-century observations, it has been recorded in historical chronicles and artworks for millennia. Its predictable orbit and spectacular tail make it the archetypal comet in Western culture.

Its orbital period is 75 to 76 years, and its passages have been documented in Chinese, Babylonian, and European records going back to at least 240 BCE. Edmund Halley, in 1705, used Newton's laws to calculate that comets observed in 1531, 1607, and 1682 were returns of the same object, predicted to reappear in 1758. His groundbreaking work revolutionized comet science by applying celestial mechanics to predict its periodicity.

The nucleus is composed of rock and dirty ice — a low-density, fragile body roughly 15 kilometers long. Its outgassing coma can extend to millions of kilometers. The comet's last perihelion was in 1986, and its next passage is expected in 2061. This makes it the only comet most people will see twice in their lifetime.

Halley's Comet was depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry in 1066 as an ill omen attending the Norman conquest. Comets were thought to presage royal deaths and calamities. The comet is also the radiant source for two meteor showers — the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October — both caused by debris left along its orbit. As the prototype of the periodic comet, Halley remains the most accessible example of cometary behavior.
